name: Angal Heneng
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Rule, Joan 1965. 'A comparison of certain phonemes of the languages of the Mendi and Nembi Valleys, Southern Highlands, Papua' (Glottolog doctype: phonology)
earlier_scan.note: Only phonology in Glottolog refs; not online. SIL OPD for akh, if any, blocked (not reachable by automated download).

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. & Joice Franklin. 1978. A Kewa dictionary, with supplementary grammatical and anthropological materials. Pacific Linguistics C-53. Section 4.2 'Mendi vowels', pp. 82-90 (= Franklin 1974, Kivung 7/3: 167-77).
sources.note: About Mendi Proper (Angal, anga1293) but names the Wola/Augu/Nipa dialects (p. 83 fn.) and reports Schlatter's and Reeson's seven-vowel phonemicisations of the Nipa (West) dialect (pp. 83 fn., 87). Only stress-related remark: /a/ 'has an allophone [ʌ] which occurs word finally in unstressed syllables' (p. 83; cf. p. 86). No rule for where stress falls. References (p. 90) name Reeson & Reeson n.d. 'Angal Heneng Language Learning Programme' MS 29 pp. and Rule & Rule 1960 'The Mendi Alphabet'.

sources.citation: Makom Tema Ebe Waeb Bisao O: The Gospel of Mark in Angal Heneng. 1967. Canberra: British and Foreign Bible Society in Australia.
sources.note: Scripture text only; no alphabet or pronunciation note.

sources.citation: Rosetta Project. n.d. Angal Heneng Swadesh list (akh). archive.org item rosettaproject_akh_swadesh-1.
sources.note: About 30 words, some carrying acute accents (andá 'big', kejép 'blood', karún 'cut', evé 'good', lurúk 'hit'); no source, key or explanation of the marks.

sources.citation: Schlatter, Vic. 1960. A preliminary sketch of the Wala verb. 14 pp. typescript. Nipa: Apostolic Christian Mission. (Glottolog ref 589413)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: First-hand on the Nipa/Wala dialect (fn. 1: Wala = speech of the Waal Aol near Nipa Patrol Station, c. 20,000 speakers). Verb morphology only; no mention of stress, tone, accent or syllables anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent found nothing).

sources.citation: Niles, Don & Alan Rumsey. 2011. Introducing Highlands sung tales. In Rumsey & Niles (eds), Sung tales from the Papua New Guinea Highlands, 1-38. Canberra: ANU E Press.
sources.note: p. 28: 'The Karinj speak the Aklal Heneng dialect of Angal Heneng'; musical notes on Karinj enj pp. 15-16. Nothing on Angal word stress.
sources.venue: Sung tales from the Papua New Guinea Highlands

sources.citation: Reithofer, Hans. 2011. Skywalkers and cannibals: Chanted tales among the Angal. In Alan Rumsey & Don Niles (eds), Sung tales from the Papua New Guinea Highlands, 207-245. Canberra: ANU E Press. DOI 10.22459/STPNGH.08.2011.10
sources.note: Karinj = Aklal Heneng / Pi Heneng dialect of Angal Heneng. p. 221 n. 19: ip 'water/river' and the immediate singular imperative of 'to come' are 'distinguished by tone only' (evidence of lexical tone); p. 231 n. 28: 'no language manual or grammar exists for Aklal Heneng'. Nothing on word stress; pp. 231-232 'Lines, melody, and pitch' concerns sung-tale melody.
sources.venue: Sung tales from the Papua New Guinea Highlands

sources.citation: Sillitoe, Paul. 1995/1998. An ethnobotanical account of the plant resources / vegetation communities of the Wola region, Southern Highlands Province, Papua New Guinea (BioStor scans).
sources.note: No language or orthography note; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Sillitoe, Paul. 1979. Give and take: Exchange in Wola society. Canberra: ANU Press. 'A Note on the Wola Language', pp. xi-xiv. (Glottolog ref 435206)
sources.note: p. xi: 'An accurate linguistic study of the Wola language remains to be made.' Table 1 (pp. xii-xiii) is a practical consonant/vowel orthography for the Was river dialect, built partly on Rule 1965: 99-100. Nothing on stress, tone or accent.

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 1975. Comments on Proto-Engan. In Wurm (ed.), PL C-38, 263-275.
sources.note: a full-text search for stress/accent: general remark that tone disambiguates present-day minimal pairs in Engan; nothing on Angal Heneng stress.

sources.citation: Wurm, S. A. 1975. Eastern Central Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 1, 461-526. Pacific Linguistics C-38.

sources.citation: Madden, B. n.d. An introduction to Mendi grammar. Unpublished MS, 92 pp. (listed in the anga1293 check)

sources.note: The only substantial grammar of any Angal variety known; concerns Mendi (East Angal, anga1293) rather than akh, but a 92-page grammar would carry a phonology chapter with a stress statement transferable with a dialect caveat.
